content: Bartholin's abscess refers to the accumulation of pus that results in a swollen lump in one of the Bartholin's glands, which are located on either side of the vaginal opening. Symptoms of Bartholin's Abscess: A tender lump on one side of the vaginal opening. Fever. Pain during sexual intercourse. Causes of Bartholin's Abscess: A Bartholin's abscess develops when the duct of the gland becomes blocked. This blockage leads to the accumulation of fluid within the gland, which can subsequently become infected. In some cases, fluid may build up over several years before an abscess forms. However, the abscess often develops rapidly over a few days, becoming hot, swollen, and painful. Activities that exert pressure on the vulva, such as walking or sitting, can cause severe pain. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: You should contact your healthcare provider if you notice a painful, swollen lump on the labia near the vaginal opening that does not improve within 2–3 days of home treatment. Immediate medical attention is also necessary if the pain is severe and interferes with daily activities. Diagnosis: A pelvic examination will typically reveal an enlarged and tender Bartholin's gland. In older women, a biopsy may be recommended to rule out the possibility of a tumor. Any vaginal discharge or fluid drainage will be sent to a laboratory for analysis. Treatment Options: Warm Water Soaks: Soaking in warm water four times a day for several days can provide relief and may cause the abscess to open and drain on its own. However, the opening is often very small and may close quickly before complete drainage occurs. Surgical Drainage: A small surgical incision can fully drain the abscess, offering the most significant relief and fastest recovery. This procedure can be performed under local anesthesia in a doctor's office. A catheter (tube) may be placed to allow continued drainage while the area heals. Antibiotics: Antibiotics may be prescribed, but they are generally not necessary if the abscess is properly drained. Marsupialization: Women with recurrent abscesses may consider a procedure called marsupialization, which involves surgically creating a small, permanent opening to facilitate gland drainage. This procedure may also be recommended for women with large, persistent Bartholin's cysts. Gland Removal: If abscesses recur frequently, your healthcare provider may suggest removing the Bartholin's glands. Medical Care Locations: You can seek treatment for Bartholin's abscess at hospitals or clinics equipped to handle such conditions. Prognosis: The likelihood of full recovery is excellent. However, approximately 10% of cases may experience recurrence. It is essential to treat any vaginal infections diagnosed concurrently with the abscess. Possible Complications: A chronic Bartholin's duct cyst may develop. In women over the age of 40, a swollen Bartholin's gland may indicate a rare cancerous tumor in the gland. Prevention: Bartholin's abscess can occur without any identifiable cause, and there is no specific way to prevent it.
